title: Tax audits and spending limits: more than an oversight measure

shots.narration: Proposition forty-one combines audits with changes to state spending-limit rules. A special tax dedicates its money to a particular purpose, unlike revenue that can be used generally. The measure concerns new or increased state special taxes.
shots.headline: What is a special tax?

shots.narration: California already has an independent state auditor and a constitutional spending limit. This proposal adds reviews at particular stages and could restrict the ability to exempt new special-tax spending from that limit.
shots.headline: Two parts of the proposal

shots.narration: Imagine a program manager proposing a dedicated funding measure.
shots.headline: Before a new tax reaches voters

shots.narration: Suppose a citizen initiative proposes a new tax for a public program. After supporters collect a quarter of the required signatures, the auditor would review the program, even though the initiative might never qualify.
shots.headline: Review starts before ballot qualification

shots.narration: An auditor examines how the program uses its money.
shots.headline: Information before a funding decision

shots.narration: If the initiative reaches the ballot, voters receive an audit summary in the voter guide. That could provide useful information, but producing the review still takes staff and money.
shots.headline: An additional source of voter information

shots.narration: The initial audit must identify ways to reduce annual program costs by ten percent. Identifying options is not the same as delivering savings or proving that services can stay unchanged.
shots.headline: A recommendation is not a guaranteed saving
items: Implementation and service effects still matter

shots.narration: Programs funded by new or increased special taxes approved after January first, twenty twenty-six, would also face recurring audits every four years. Approved taxes generally fund the audits; unsuccessful initiatives can leave costs to the General Fund.
shots.headline: Who pays for the reviews?

shots.narration: The analyst expects audit costs in the low millions annually, growing over time, plus voter-guide expenses. Savings depend on decisions to implement effective recommendations, so the overall fiscal result is unknown.
shots.headline: Costs are estimated; net savings are not

shots.narration: The spending-limit provisions are a separate issue. Prop forty-one could block Prop forty if both pass and forty-one receives more yes votes, subject to how courts interpret their conflict.
shots.headline: The connection to Prop 40

shots.narration: A voter might want evidence of efficiency before approving new dedicated taxes, and regular follow-up afterward. They may also prefer keeping new revenue within spending constraints. Those are two distinct reasons to consider, rather than assuming audits are the entire measure.
shots.headline: The case for YES

shots.narration: You might ask whether extra reviews justify their cost.
shots.headline: Your question: oversight or added constraints?

shots.narration: Another voter could favor oversight but object to mandatory reviews of measures that never qualify, or to limits on funding flexibility. They may also oppose the effect on Prop forty. An audit requirement does not automatically mean waste is eliminated.
shots.headline: The case for NO

shots.narration: In the September PPIC survey of likely voters, 51 percent said yes, 44 percent no, and 5 percent were unsure. These are dated survey results, not votes already cast.
shots.headline: September snapshot: PPIC

shots.narration: A later September Berkeley survey found 37 percent yes, 33 percent no, and 30 percent undecided. Question wording and methods differ, so comparing polls does not by itself establish a trend.
shots.headline: September snapshot: Berkeley IGS
shots.poll_note: Berkeley IGS · Sept 15–20, 2026 · likely voters · about ±2 points

shots.narration: Yes adds audits and spending-limit provisions; no keeps the current framework. Visit our website for the fuller explanation, source links, and official voter guide. Compare the tradeoffs, then make your own informed choice.
shots.headline: Explore the full explanation
